title: The Second Letter of Peter
subtitle: Petrou B, “Second of Peter”
description: A farewell letter in Peter’s name, written by one who knows he must soon lay aside “this tent of a body”, so that his readers will remember what matters most. God’s divine power has given us every gift that leads to life and godliness, and promises by which we may share in the divine nature; so add to faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, affection and love. The apostles were eyewitnesses on the holy mountain, not tellers of clever stories; false teachers will come, and God knows how to rescue the godly; and to the scoffers who ask “Where is this promise of his coming?”, the answer that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, that he is patient, not wanting anyone to be destroyed, and that we look for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Second Letter of Peter?
qa.answer: The twenty-second book of the New Testament, a short farewell letter in which Peter, expecting to die soon, reminds his readers of the truth they have received. It urges them to grow in goodness, knowledge and love, warns against false teachers who promise freedom but live in greed and corruption, and answers those who mock the promise of Christ’s return: God’s seeming delay is his patience, giving people time to repent, and the day of the Lord will surely come. It ends with a call to keep growing in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ (3:18).

qa.question: Did Peter write 2 Peter?
qa.answer: The letter names “Simeon Peter” as its author, recalls the transfiguration as something he saw, and calls itself his second letter. But its authorship has been questioned since early times: it is rarely quoted before the third century, Eusebius listed it among the books some disputed, and Jerome noted that its style differs from 1 Peter. Many modern scholars think a follower wrote it after Peter’s death, as a last testament in his name; others hold that Peter wrote it, perhaps with a different secretary, shortly before his martyrdom in the mid-60s. The church received it as Scripture after long consideration.

qa.question: What does “a single day is like a thousand years” mean in 2 Peter 3:8?
qa.answer: Peter is answering scoffers who say the promise of Christ’s coming has failed because so much time has passed. Echoing Psalm 90, he says that God does not measure time as people do: “in the Lord’s sight a single day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a single day.” The point is not a formula for calculating dates, but that the Lord is not slow in keeping his promise. He is being patient, “He does not want anyone to be destroyed, but wants all people to turn back in repentance” (3:9).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
